Opening Note
It is with great pleasure that we welcome you to the 38th edition of the European Conference
on Real-Time Systems (ECRTS). Owing to its long tradition, ECRTS has established itself as
a premier event for the real-time and embedded systems community. Indeed, ECRTS serves
as a top-ranking platform, comparable to RTAS and RTSS, for researchers, practitioners,
and industry professionals to exchange ideas and advance the field of real-time systems.
We are thrilled to host this year’s ECRTS in Lund, Sweden. Johan Eker (Lund University)
serves as the general chair. The technical program has been curated by the Technical Program
Committee (TPC) chair Angeliki Kritikakou from Univ. Rennes, Inria, IRISA in France to
foster a collaborative environment that encourages innovation and knowledge sharing.
Since its inception, ECRTS has been a fertile ground for innovative initiatives to boost
inclusiveness, improve the evaluation process, and broaden participation in the research
community. This year, we have continued the well-established tradition of open-access
proceedings using Dagstuhl LIPIcs (Leibniz International Proceedings in Informatics); we
have continued to offer the authors of accepted papers an optional artifact evaluation process.
ECRTS’ double-blind submission policies incorporate provisions allowing authors to freely
publish pre-prints of their work before or after submission to ECRTS.
Furthermore, this year, we have introduced two tracks. ECRTS welcomes both theoretical
and practical contributions through the “Foundations, Methodologies and Theory track”,
which welcomes contributions advancing the theory, methodology, and formal analysis of realtime and time-sensitive systems, and the “Tools, Implementations and Practical Experience
track”, which highlights tools, implementations, and real-world experience, including tools supporting analysis, scheduling, or design of time-sensitive systems, implementations and prototypes, industrial case studies, and lessons learned from real deployments. We have defined a set
of evaluation criteria for the two tracks (https://www.ecrts.org/evaluation-criteria/).
We also continued for the second year the Shadow Technical Program Committee (STPC).
The primary objective of the STPC is to create an immersive training platform for young
and emerging researchers who might go on to become future reviewers. Participation in the
STPC aims to offer early-career researchers hands-on experience in the peer-review process,
developing and refining their evaluation and reviewing skills under the guidance of more
experienced reviewers in an inclusive environment. Under the guidance of Tomasz Kloda
(LAAS-CNRS, France) in the role of STPC chair, STPC members conducted a parallel review
process of the same articles evaluated by the main TPC – on an opt-in basis for the authors.
They were then provided the anonymized reviews that TPC members produced for the same
set of papers. We sincerely thank Tomasz for making this possible.
We are thankful to Bryan Ward (Vanderbilt University) and Federico Aromolo (Scuola
Superiore Sant’Anna), who served as chairs of this year’s Artifact Evaluation (AE) committee.
This year, the AE committee was comprised of 10 international experts who evaluated eleven
submissions. Papers approved by the AE committee are identified in this proceedings with a

Continuing a long-standing tradition, this year’s ECRTS also includes an industrial

the WATERS workshop and has become a symbiotically integrated part of the main ECRTS
program. Our thanks go to Michael Roitzsch (Barkhausen Institute) and Peter Wägemann

(Scuola Superiore Sant’Anna), who served as the publicity chair for this year’s edition and
introduced several new outreach channels.

perfect order. Cecilia Edelberg and Monika Rasmusson have been in charge of all booking
and budget matters. We are truly grateful for all their hard work.
Finally, and perhaps most importantly, we would like to express our deep gratitude
toward all the authors who submitted their work to ECRTS 2026. Unfortunately, employing
a rigorous selection process means that some works will not be given the opportunity to
appear in the conference program. Nonetheless, regardless of whether they are accepted or
rejected, all the submitted articles contribute to setting the quality bar of the conference
and are therefore vital for its existence. All in all, we are positively impressed by the general
quality of this year’s submissions. The final selection, which we hereby present to you, excels
both in terms of breadth and depth. As such, we look forward to seeing you in Lund and
sincerely hope that you will enjoy ECRTS 2026!

Paper Submission and Selection
Selection Process
The submission timeline was defined as follows. Authors of original papers could submit
their work for consideration at ECRTS with a submission deadline set on February 26,
2026. A week-long online discussion phase preceded the TPC meeting. The purpose of the
discussion phase was to understand the existence of a consensus (or lack thereof) between
reviewers before heading to the TPC meeting. The per-paper discussions during this phase
were facilitated by discussion leads selected by the TPC chair. The TPC meeting was held
virtually on Zoom on April 16, 2026. At the beginning of the selection process, four papers
were identified to have a conflict of interest (CoI) with the TPC chair. The entire process
for these papers was handled by Daniel Casini (Scuola Superiore Sant’Anna). The authors
were notified of the result of the TPC peer-review process on April 20, 2025. The possible
outcomes for manuscripts at this stage were: (1) Accepted, (2) Rejected, or (3) Shepherded.
A paper receiving an Accepted decision was immediately slated to appear in this proceedings. Conversely, a manuscript receiving a Rejected decision was deemed unsuitable
for publication at ECRTS 2026 due to either a scope mismatch or foundational technical
shortcomings. Finally, the reviewers had the option to recommend a paper for a Shepherded
decision. This case was reserved for papers that were deemed promising by the reviewers but
that were perceived as not quite ready to be accepted as is. A paper receiving a Shepheded
decision was considered conditionally accepted. It was assigned (1) a clear set of shepherding
requirements to be addressed by the authors and (2) a shepherd from the pool of reviewers
tasked to ensure that the requirements are met in the revised version of the manuscript. The
deadline for shepherds to finalize their decision was set as May 8, 2026.
Upon conclusion of the TPC meeting, all the papers received a final decision, as described
above. Each paper also received a meta-review summarizing the nature of the discussion
entertained by the reviewers and the chairs during the offline and online phases.
In line with the inclusiveness goals of ECRTS, no specific acceptance rate was targeted by
the TPC chair. The reviewers were given explicit guidance to appropriately use Shepherded
decisions in case of promising papers with fixable flaws. It is always challenging to ensure the
perfect adherence of the entire TPC to the established guidelines. Nonetheless, we sincerely
hope that all the authors of those papers that received a Rejected decision will be able to use
the provided feedback to improve and re-submit their work to future venues.

Submission and Selection Statistics
The 38th edition of ECRTS received a total of 63 valid submissions. The overall number of
submissions corresponded to an 14.5% increase compared to ECRTS 2025. Out of the total
of 63 submissions, the TPC finally accepted 23 full papers for publication. This represents
an acceptance rate of about 36.5%. Once again, this was not a targeted acceptance rate but
rather the result of an organic selection process. By the conclusion of the TPC meeting,
all papers received at least four full reviews. After the TPC meeting, 13 papers received
an Accepted decision (∼20%); 40 received a Rejected decision (63.5%); and 10 received
a Shepherded decision (∼16.5%). Of the papers that received a Shepherded decision, 10
(∼100%) were subsequently accepted to appear at the conference.

Paper Submission and Selection

Alignment between Evaluation Committees
Out of the 63 total ECRTS 2026 submissions, the authors of 40 submissions (∼63.5%) opted
to have their work also submitted for evaluation to the STPC. This is an excellent rate, as it
increased by (∼23.5%) compared to the first STPC happened in 2025. Of the 40 submissions,
15 submissions received at least three reviews, 21 of them received two reviews, and 4 of them
received 1 review, resulting in a total of 92 reviews. This highlights an excellent engagement
record, considering that STPC members had, in most cases, no track record of previous
involvement in similar committees. The STPC was composed of 37 members: PhD students,
postdocs, assistant professors, and both academic and industry researchers.
Having an STPC operating in parallel with respect to the main TPC allows for an
interesting introspection into the level of objectiveness of the overall evaluation process. In
particular, we have analyzed the level of alignment between the two evaluations (TPC vs.
STPC). Out of the 40 papers evaluated by the STPC, 27 (67.5%) received the same outcome
in both committees. This ratio was computed considering the final decisions of the TPC
at the end of the shepherding phase. We consider the decisions of the two committees as
“aligned” in those cases where (1) the TPC recommended an Accepted decision and the STPC
provided a positive-leaning decision (Accepted or Shepherded); or (2) both PC recommended
a Rejected decision. Out of the 40 reviewed submissions, the STPC recommended the
acceptance of 18 papers, including 7 conditional acceptances. This corresponds to the STPC
acceptance rate of 45%, compared to 36.5% for the main TPC.

Critical-Section Granularity for Multi-Resource
Systems with Nested Critical Sections
Catherine E. Nemitz #
Davidson College, NC, USA

Tanya Amert #
Carleton College, NC, USA

Jonad Pulaj #
Davidson College NC, USA

Abstract
Typical models of resource-sharing real-time tasks provide the worst-case task execution time and
the duration of each critical section during which a resource is accessed. Such models abstract away
the detailed behavior of a task, which may make several individual accesses within a single critical
section, incurring access overhead once for the entire critical section. Considering a more fine-grained
model with individual access and non-access segments at the forefront gives more control in the
system design process; choosing how accesses are grouped into critical sections enables balancing
trade-offs between overhead and blocking based on other system parameters, including task deadlines.
This paper presents an optimal approach for multi-resource systems that allow any given task to use
up to two resources, including support for nested critical sections. This is achieved by extending
analysis to multiple resources and constructing a Quadratically-Constrained Integer Program to
determine critical sections. This approach is compared to heuristics on the basis of schedulability
and its runtime is explored. Further extension to support more resources per task is discussed.
2012 ACM Subject Classification Computer systems organization → Real-time systems; Software
and its engineering → Mutual exclusion; Software and its engineering → Synchronization
Keywords and phrases Real-time systems, shared resources, fixed-priority scheduling, schedulability
Digital Object Identifier 10.4230/LIPIcs.ECRTS.2026.1

1

Introduction

Models of real-time systems necessarily abstract away details of system implementation to
enable application of existing scheduling theory. This abstraction includes masking details
surrounding access to any shared resource, such as a GPU or a region of shared memory,
which may require mutually exclusive access while a task is in a critical section for that
resource. Such details are often reduced to a pair of related components: the duration of
each critical section for a task’s use of a resource, and the extent to which a given task could
incur blocking, the delay a task experiences while a lower-priority task is executing.
While a critical-section duration in an abstract task model might be assumed to model
exactly the time needed to access a given resource, recent work has found that consecutive
accesses to a GPU have a reduced duration compared to those same computations occurring
with possible intermediate workload by as much as 100µs [2, 3]. Indeed, a variety of shared
resources can have associated overhead, additional time required for the first access in a series.
In addition to modeling the additional time for non-consecutive GPU accesses, overhead can
also model the time it takes to execute the protocol coordinating access to a shared resource.
If the overhead approaches the duration of an access itself, as in the case of GPU accesses,
being able to perform multiple such accesses in succession becomes an attractive option.

Critical-Section Granularity for Multi-Resource Systems

Thus, we consider a fine-grained model that provides details regarding a task’s individual
resource accesses; these accesses must then be converted into critical sections before runtime.
Multiple accesses (e.g., an individual write to memory or a single computation on a GPU)
are often grouped into a single critical section, as has been observed in prior work [2, 3].
By reasoning at a more fine-grained level, we consider which accesses should be grouped
to form each critical section and balance these decisions based on the overhead, blocking, and
broader schedulability implications for the task system as a whole. By adding this complexity
to the model, we can manage the trade-offs between the reduced overhead one task may
incur by grouping multiple accesses into a single critical section with the higher blocking
that this grouping could force another task to incur.
Prior work investigated theses trade-offs in a limited scope, for systems with a single
resource [3] and systems with multiple resources that disallow nesting (i.e., holding multiple
resources concurrently) [10]. We build on these results to support systems with any number
of resources that allow critical-section nesting in which each task accesses up to two resources.
Contributions. We provide necessary background on the task model and related work
(Sec. 2). We then extend previous analysis of systems with a single resource to analysis for
multi-resource systems and show that straightforward extensions to a greedy approach are not
optimal (Sec. 3). Instead, we build a Quadratically-Constrained Integer Program that allows
exploring different combinations of accesses into critical section (Sec. 4). We then present
an experimental evaluation on the basis of schedulability and runtime (Sec. 5). We also
discuss how all possible combinations of accesses into critical sections could be generated and
considered for tasks that use more than two resources (Sec. 6) before concluding (Sec. 7).

2

Background

In this section, we provide needed background and intuition for the critical-section granularity
trade-off. We then explain the approach from prior work that groups critical sections in
systems with a single shared resource.

2.1

Task Model

We consider a system of n tasks executing on a uniprocessor platform.1 Each task τi
corresponds to a sequence of jobs released at least Ti time units apart, each with a deadline
Di ≤ Ti time units after release. We assume tasks are scheduled according to a fixedpriority scheduling policy, and that tasks are indexed in order of decreasing priority, e.g.,
D1 ≤ D2 ≤ ... ≤ Dn for Deadline Monotonic.

2.2

Resource Model

During execution, jobs may require access to one or more shared resources, e.g., shared
memory objects or hardware accelerators. Here we assume a locking protocol is used to
ensure mutually exclusive use of these shared resources. When a job needs to utilize a shared
resource, it issues a request to the protocol; the job then acquires the lock for the resource
and is granted access, or it waits until it acquires the lock. After the lock-holding job finishes
its use of the resource, it releases the lock.

1

The presented approach can also be applied to a single processor of a partitioned multiprocessor system
provided the resources used by tasks on that processor are not used on any other processor and there is
no other source of interprocessor delay to incorporate.


C. E. Nemitz, T. Amert, and J. Pulaj

1:3

The interval between a job’s acquisition and release of the lock is its critical section. We
refer to the worst-case duration of any critical section for resource ℒk by a job of task τi
as Lki . A critical section of task τi is non-nested if no other critical section of τi overlaps
with it. Two critical sections of task τi that overlap are nested; we require critical sections to
be properly nested, i.e., one is entirely contained within another.
We focus on priority-inversion blocking (blocking), which is when task τj is blocked by a
task τi of lower priority (i.e., j < i), e.g., when τj waits for access to a resource that τi holds.

2.3

Priority Ceiling Protocol

We assume the use of the Priority Ceiling Protocol (PCP) [11] to arbitrate shared resource
access. The PCP requires properly nested critical sections and relies on the notion of a
priority ceiling, which is defined as the highest priority of any task that uses the resource.
We let 𝒽k (resp., 𝓁k ) denote the priority of the highest-priority (resp., lowest-priority) task
that uses resource ℒk . Under the PCP, a task may request resource access if its priority is
higher (i.e., its index is smaller) than that of the highest-priority task that uses any currently
held resource.
We leverage two properties of the PCP:

P2

Under the PCP, a critical section of τi for ℒk can block a job of task τj only if τi has
lower priority than τj (i.e., j < i) and the priority ceiling for ℒk is higher than or
equal to the priority of τj (i.e., 𝒽k ≤ j) [6, 11].
Each job can be blocked for at most one critical section that satisfies Rule P1 [11].

2.4

Critical-Section Granularity and Revised Task Model

P1

Each lock request for a shared resource incurs some overhead (e.g., as part of acquiring the
lock or due to a cold cache on a shared GPU). If a task holds a lock for the duration of two
accesses instead of releasing and re-acquiring it, coupling those two original sections together
into one, then one occurrence of overhead may be avoided and the worst-case execution time
(WCET, denoted Ci ) for that task is reduced. Given two or more accesses for the same
shared resource, we say those accesses are grouped together if they form a single critical
section with a single overhead incurred for all the considered accesses. Unfortunately, by
Rules P1 and P2, an increase in Lki for a task τi may result in increased blocking for a
higher-priority task τj . However, a critical section for resource ℒk with duration less than
the maximum Lki could have its duration increased up to Lki without impacting the blocking
of any higher-priority tasks, by Rule P2.
This trade-off motivated an exploration into critical-section granularity by Amert and
Nemitz [3]. In their work, they assume that the temporal distribution of accesses by each task
is known a priori; each task is modeled as an alternating sequence of access and non-access
segments, with αiν (resp., γiν ) referring to the ν-th access (resp., non-access) segment of τi .
A task can thus be represented as a tuple τi = (Ti , Γi , Ai , Λi , Di ), where Γi and Ai
represent lists of durations of non-access and access segments, respectively, Λi lists the
resource corresponding to each access segment, and |Ai | gives the number of accesses made
by task τi . We refer to the duration of an access (resp., non-access) segment as |αiν | (resp.,
|γiν |) and let Ok denote the overhead associated with resource ℒk .
▶ Example 1. Consider the task τi depicted in Fig. 1 (a), with Ai = [2, 1, 3, 2], Λi =
[ℒ1 , ℒ2 , ℒ1 , ℒ2 ], Γi = [1, 5, 2, 2, 1], O1 = 1 time unit, and O2 = 2 time units. The worst-case
duration of each segment is shown below it.

To ensure mutually exclusive accesses to the shared resources, the accesses must be

contained within the other.
The larger L1i illustrated in Fig. 1 (b) enables a reduction in Ci for τi compared to peraccess critical sections, which reduces the execution requirement for this and lower-priority
tasks, and thereby may improve system schedulability, the guarantee that all jobs of all tasks
meet their deadlines. However, this increase in critical-section duration may not be possible
if increasing L1i would block a higher-priority task enough that it misses its deadline.

Prior work [3] leveraged this approach to determine a bound on critical-section duration
in systems with a single resource using the Priority Inheritance Protocol [11] or the PCP. The
values of βj for each task τj can be used to determine the upper-bound on critical-section
duration Qi for each lower-priority task τi (i.e., j < i) such that the blocking incurred by τj
does not exceed βj . The following recurrence relation (Thm. 4.5 in [3]) computes Qi given
the blocking tolerances and critical-section-duration bounds for higher-priority tasks:

Here, 𝒽 is the index of the highest-priority task to use the resource and 𝓁 that of the lowest.
Amert and Nemitz [3] showed that it is optimal to iterate through the tasks in decreasing
priority order and assign critical sections to each in turn without needing to revisit prior
decisions (illustrated in Alg. 1). Critically, the choice of lock granularity for a particular task
can be based only on higher-priority tasks. The bound βj is computed for each higher-priority
task τj . These bounds are used to then determine Qi . A choice of assigning accesses to
critical sections for τi that minimizes its WCET is the best possible scenario for lower-priority
tasks; this minimizes the impact τi has on the response time of these tasks. This approach
of handling tasks individually in decreasing priority order is optimal in the sense that if any
assignment of accesses to critical sections will yield a schedulable task set, this approach will.

3

Greedily Grouping Accesses with Multiple Resources

In this section, we discuss why we can leverage the structure of Alg. 1 in the multi-resource
case, and thereby still consider each task in isolation. We then explore the challenges presented
by trying to apply the original greedy access-grouping algorithm from [3] to systems with
multiple shared resources.

3.1

Application to multi-resource problem

To support multiple shared resources, we begin by examining the computation of per-resource
values for βi and Qi , and then discuss why the structure of Alg. 1 still applies.

3.1.1

Computing bounds on critical-section durations

We first consider which critical sections can block a given task and use this to determine
blocking tolerance. We then shift our perspective to looking at which tasks could be blocked
by a given critical section to compute a bound on critical-section duration.

3.1.1.1

Point-of-View: The Task Being Blocked

We begin by utilizing the properties of the PCP defined in Sec. 2 to note that any blocking
actually experienced by task τj comes from a single critical section. Let Bj be the worst-case
blocking that task τj may experience due to critical sections for any resource, and let Bjk be
the worst-case blocking it may experience due to critical sections for resource ℒk .

Proof. By Rule P2, task τj can be blocked by at most one critical section. Thus, its blocking
is at most that caused by any single resource ℒk , denoted Bjk . By Rule P1, τj can only be
blocked by a critical section for ℒk belonging to a lower-priority task τi , i.e., j < i, if the
priority ceiling for ℒk is higher than or equal to the priority of τj , i.e., 𝒽k ≤ j. As no task
with priority lower than 𝓁k uses ℒk , such a task τi must satisfy j < i ≤ 𝓁k .
◀
For task systems that utilize multiple shared resources, the per-resource blocking tolerance
βjk of a given task τj separately for each resource ℒk , as shown below.
▶ Lemma 2. Under the PCP, for two resources ℒa and ℒb , the bounds βja and βjb for τj
can be computed and applied independently.
Proof. Without loss of generality, suppose that the value of βja has been established. Thus,
ensuring Bja ≤ βja gives that τj cannot be blocked by a critical section using ℒa for a duration
that would cause it to be unschedulable. Now let us consider the determination of βjb .
Because the PCP ensures each task can be blocked by at most one critical section by Rule P2,
τj cannot be blocked by both a critical section for ℒa and a separate critical section3 for ℒb .
That is, only the maximum critical-section duration over any resource ℒk impacts blocking
by Lem. 1. Therefore, the bound βjb does not depend on βja and its constraint on blocking
(Bjb ≤ βjb ) can be applied independently to the constraint on Bja .
◀
Next, we express how to determine βjk of a given task τj separately for each resource ℒk
based on its priority relative to the priorities of the highest- and lowest-priority tasks that

Similarly, by Rule P1 a critical section can block a job of task τj only if that critical

resource ℒk by Rule P1. For j in this range, if τj can tolerate blocking up to βj , then it can
tolerate blocking caused by a critical section for ℒk up to βjk = βj .

3.1.1.2

Point-of-View: The Task Causing Blocking

We now seek to derive the upper-bound on critical-section duration Qki for each resource ℒk
used by task τi given the blocking tolerance βjk for all higher-priority tasks τj . We will then
use this bound to require that Lki ≤ Qki for each resource ℒk used by task τi .
Our approach builds on that used for single-resource systems [3], which in turn built on
concepts from non-preemptive regions [12, 13]. We extend this proof structure to consider a
system with multiple resources managed by the PCP. Due to space constraints, proofs that
follow similar logic as those in previous work are condensed or omitted to allow focus on
those aspects most relevant to multiple resources under the PCP.
We begin by noting that no bound is imposed on critical sections that cannot cause
blocking, as stated in the following lemmas.
▶ Lemma 4. For any task τi satisfying i ≤ 𝒽k , Qki = ∞.
Proof. A task τi satisfying i < 𝒽k does not use resource ℒk and thus cannot block any other
task due to critical sections for ℒk . If τi satisfies i = 𝒽k , then τi is the highest-priority task
that uses ℒk , so by Rule P1, no critical sections of τi for ℒk can cause blocking.
As τi cannot cause blocking with critical sections for resource ℒk , there is no bound
imposed on the durations of those critical sections, so Qki = ∞.
◀
▶ Lemma 5. For any task τi satisfying 𝓁k < i, Qki = ∞.
Proof. If 𝓁k < i, task τi does not use and thus cannot cause blocking with resource ℒk .

◀

computes the bound Qki in terms of computed properties of higher-priority tasks.

3.1.2

Considering each task in decreasing-priority order

The correctness of Alg. 1 in the multi-resource case would be at risk if the chosen grouping
of accesses into critical sections for task τi were to impact the bound Qki used to perform the
grouping itself. However, the same reasoning used in the single-resource case (Lemma 4.13
and Corollary 4.14 in [3]) applies in our case, as each computation relies only on values
previously computed: βik and Qki depend only on properties of tasks with the same or higher
priority than that of τi , by Eqs. (1), (2), and (4) and Eq. (5), respectively, and the order in
which they are computed is unchanged from the single-resource case.
The optimality of this ordering depends on two assumptions:
1. The algorithm to group accesses into critical sections for task τi minimizes Ci .
2. Reducing Ci for a task τi can only increase the bounds on critical-section durations and
blocking tolerance for τi .
The extension of this second requirement from the single- to the multiple-resource case
follows given our consideration of each resource independently. As we shall see in the next
section, however, the greedy algorithm used for the single-resource case does not guarantee a
minimized WCET Ci for task τi . Given two shared resources, we say there is a valid grouping
of accesses into critical sections that satisfy the critical-section-duration bounds Lk ≤ Qk for
each applicable resource ℒk , if there is no nesting, or if the access segments for the outer
resource are grouped together and the grouping (or groupings if present) of the inner resource
yield a properly nested critical section. We define an optimal grouping to be a valid grouping
that yields a minimal WCET.

3.2

Extending the greedy access-grouping algorithm to multiple
resources

We begin by considering the greedy algorithm used to group accesses into critical sections
for single-resource systems, as well as two extensions to multiple resources:
SingleResourceGreedy: This algorithm, proven optimal for a single resource in [3],
is essentially the next-fit bin-packing algorithm with a bin capacity of Qi and accesses
considered in index order. A new critical section for access αiν is initialized with weight
O + |αiν |. When adding a later access αiξ to a critical section, the weight is incremented
by |γiξ−1 | + |αiξ |.
GreedyNonNested: This algorithm utilizes SingleResourceGreedy for any contiguous sequence of accesses for the same resource. It therefore never produces nested
critical sections, but it is very straightforward to implement and a direct extension of
SingleResourceGreedy.
GreedyNested: This variant of SingleResourceGreedy considers each access in
turn, but adds the appropriate overhead each time an access to a new resource is added to
a critical section. This is much more complex to implement, e.g., with a stack to ensure
proper nesting of critical sections.

As in prior work, we say that an access-grouping algorithm is optimal if it finds a
grouping that minimizes the WCET Ci of the task τi under consideration while ensuring
schedulability, if such a grouping exists. Unfortunately, neither of these extensions is optimal
in the multiple-resource setting.
▶ Lemma 8. The algorithms GreedyNonNested and GreedyNested are not optimal.
Proof. Consider the same task from Ex. 1, shown in Fig. 2 with different groupings of
accesses into critical sections. Let Q1i = 16 time units and Q2i = 14 time units.
Fig. 2 (a) depicts the critical sections chosen by GreedyNonNested. No two consecutive
accesses are for the same resource, so none are grouped. Each access incurs overhead, leading
to a WCET of Ci = 25 time units.
If instead GreedyNested is used, we combine the first three accesses into a single
critical section, as shown in Fig. 2 (b). We cannot include the fourth access in this critical
section as it would require L1i = 20 > Q1i to maintain proper nesting. We avoid one instance
of overhead O1 , giving a WCET of Ci = 24 time units.
If instead we assign the first access to its own critical section and group the remaining
three, as shown in Fig. 2 (c), then the higher overhead O2 is incurred only once and we have
Ci = 23 time units. Neither GreedyNonNested or GreedyNested produces this optimal
assignment of accesses to critical sections.
◀
Despite the complexity required to maintain proper nesting in GreedyNested, it is not
guaranteed to find the optimal grouping.
We have seen that multiple greedy heuristics that extend the SingleResourceGreedy
algorithm can lead to non-optimal critical sections. Next, we explore an optimization-based
approach that is optimal for tasks using up to two resources.

4

Formulating an Optimization Problem

In this section, we construct a Quadratically-Constrained Integer Program to group accesses
into (potentially nested) critical sections for a given task. When determining critical sections
for an entire task set, a separate optimization problem is created for each resource-using
task, corresponding to each call to GroupAccesses in Alg. 1. As we consider only a single
task at a time, we omit the task index in this section.

ECRTS 2026


1:10

Critical-Section Granularity for Multi-Resource Systems

Our approach, which we refer to as MultiResOpt, assumes any given task uses at
most two shared resources and requires pre-designating which resource will be the outer or
inner resource in any nested critical section. We begin by arguing that this choice does not
artificially eliminate potential solutions; we show that if accesses can be grouped into critical
sections satisfying Lk ≤ Qk while minimizing C, then there is also a solution in which the
outer critical section is fixed. We then introduce our optimization problem and construct
constraints separately for the inner resource and outer resource.

4.1

Pre-designating the inner and outer resource

We focus on a two-resource problem in which a task uses exactly two shared resources. For a
two-resource problem, we choose a resource to be the outer resource (denoted with k = A) as
opposed to the inner (denoted with k = B) based on the values of Qk to ensure QA ≥ QB . We
remind the reader that valid (hence optimal) groupings satisfy the critical-section-duration
bounds Lk ≤ Qk for each resource ℒk used by the task.
▶ Lemma 9. If a two-resource problem admits an optimal grouping with nested critical
sections, then there exists an optimal grouping with the outer resource fixed.
Proof. Given a two-resource problem that admits an optimal grouping with nested critical
sections, assume with no loss of generality that QA ≥ QB holds.
First, suppose we have an optimal grouping in which a critical section has ℒB as the
outer resource and ℒA as the inner one. By our assumption that QA ≥ QB , it is possible for
all accesses for ℒA within this critical section for ℒB to be grouped into one critical section
for ℒA . In fact, they must all be grouped together, or else additional overhead for ℒA would
be incurred, rendering this grouping non-optimal. Thus, given a critical section with ℒB as
the outer resource, all accesses for resource ℒA are contained in a single inner critical section.
Second, we show that given a valid grouping in which a single critical section for resource
ℒA is nested within a critical section for ℒB , then an alternate solution with the critical
section for ℒB nested within a critical section for ℒA is also a valid grouping and does
not change C. Let X represent the duration of the outer critical section for ℒB excluding
overhead. Then the total duration is LB = OB + OA + X, which must be at most QB by
virtue of being a valid grouping. Thus, OB + OA + X ≤ QB ≤ QA . Changing the order
of resource acquisition to make ℒA the outer resource results in a critical-section duration
of LA = OA + OB + X ≤ QA , which yields a valid grouping. Since no other computation
time of the task has changed, the outer critical-section duration stays the same, hence C is
unchanged as further illustrated in Fig. 3. Applying these two observations to every critical
section with ℒB as the outer resource, we arrive at the desired optimal grouping.

Overview of MultiResOpt Algorithm

As an optimal assignment of accesses to critical sections minimizes the WCET for our task,
this provides the objective function for our Quadratically-Constrained Integer Program:
minimize C

(6)

We introduce a set of binary decision variables to indicate, for each access, if that access
is combined with the previous access as part of a critical section for the specified resource.
For a task that uses two resources, a given access may belong to a critical section of one
(non-nested) or both (nested), so we track each decision separately. We use additional
variables to capture the resulting critical-section durations.
In the remainder of this section, we present constraints for grouping accesses first of the
inner and then the outer resource, including constraints used to determine critical-section
durations for each. Finally, we constrain the critical-section durations and the total task
duration C based on the values of decision variables and given the bounds Qk . We summarize
all constraints in Tbl. 3 at the end of this section.

Constraints on critical-section duration

Each individual partial duration of a critical section must be at most the relevant bound on
the critical-section duration, Qk .
∀ν, k ∈ {A, B}, yνk ≤ Qk

(27)

at most the bound on the critical-section duration ensures that the entire duration of any
critical section is at most the provided bound Qk .

5

Evaluation

We evaluate approaches on the basis of schedulability to capture the extent to which each
finds groupings of accesses to critical sections that yield a schedulable task set. We compare
our approach to heuristic approaches under task set generation methods as described below.


C. E. Nemitz, T. Amert, and J. Pulaj

5.1

1:19

Approaches

MultiResOpt is the approach presented above that requires computing Q for each resource
(Sec. 3), selecting inner and outer resources (Sec. 4.1), and constructing and solving the
optimization problem. If a given task uses only a single resource, we treat it as the outer
resource and set a different resource with critical-section duration bound of zero as the inner
resource. To avoid potential numerical issues in the solver, when some Qk = ∞, we use an
upper bound on the entire task duration as a bound on Q.
NeverCombine is a simple heuristic that transforms each access into an individual
critical section which includes the access duration and the respective overhead.
AlwaysCombine combines, for accesses all of the same resource, all accesses and any
interleaving non-access segments into a single critical section along with the corresponding
overhead. To support multiple resources, a more nuanced approach is taken based on how
accesses are distributed throughout the task: if all accesses for one resource come before any
access of the other, two critical sections are formed, one per resource. For tasks in which
accesses for different resources mostly alternate, we create critical sections for each resource
such that one critical section is nested within the other. We choose the resource for the outer
critical section to have a larger (or equal) sum of overhead and duration from its first access
to its last (including any intermediate non-access segments). The outer critical section begins
at the first access for either resource and ends at the last while ensuring proper nesting. The
inner critical section spans from the first to last accesses of the chosen inner resource.
GreedyNonNested operates as a heuristic as described in Sec. 3.2. It uses the approach
presented in Sec. 3 to extend to multiple resources and creates non-nested critical sections in
a manner that builds directly on prior work for a single resource [3].
NOLOCK uses the sum of access and non-access segment durations for each task’s WCET
and depicts the baseline schedulability without accounting for any overhead or blocking
caused by critical sections to illustrate the inherent, non-resource-related, schedulability
challenges.

5.2

Experiment Types

We conducted experiments by generating synthetic task sets with SchedCAT [1] with varying
attributes and then checking the schedulability under Deadline Monotonic with the PCP
when using each method described above. For any range specified, a given sample was
selected uniformly at random. Per-task utilizations were selected from light (0.001–0.1) or
medium (0.1–0.4) ranges. Task periods were chosen from short (3ms–33ms) or moderate
(10ms–100ms) periods. Deadlines were selected to be from 40% to 60% of task periods.
The percentage of tasks selected to use a shared resource was chosen from
{60%, 80%, 100%}. The probability that a given resource-using task used only one resource was chosen from {0, 0.5, 0.85}; otherwise it used two resources. If a task used two
resources, it was possible for the selected grouping to result in one or more nested critical
sections. Based on observations of the Linux kernel and the frequency of non-nested locks,
we included the probability 0.85 [5]. Of course, it would be possible for a task to use two
resources and not have any nested critical sections. Which resources a task used are selected
randomly from those available, and we considered systems to have a total number of resources
selected from {2, 4, 8}. For each task, inspiration was taken from observed GPU access times
and overhead [2, 3], so access duration was selected from (10µs–200µs) and overheads were
set to 100µs. For each system utilization, 100 task systems were generated. Additional detail
about the generation of individual access and non-access segments is given below.

Figure 7 Schedulability results.

Single-Resource Access Generation. Up to eight access segments were generated for a task
using a single resource. Each non-access segment between these was given duration half of
that of an access segment. The total duration of these access segments and the interleaving
non-access segments was constrained to be at most 95% of the selected WCET for the task.
If eight access segments would exceed this, the largest possible number is chosen instead.
In extreme cases, it may not be possible to have an access segment for a chosen task. The
non-access segments before the first access and after the last are of equal duration, matching
the time needed to fill the remainder of the worst-case execution time, rounded down.
Alternating Accesses. For the alternating access-generation pattern, a similar approach
is applied as with a single resource. For a task using two resources, accesses are generated
in pairs, alternating accesses between the two selected resources, up to eight pairs (or the
number that will fit within 95% of the WCET, as described above). The access duration for
each resource is selected independently.
Access Groups. For the grouped access pattern, a similar structure is applied, but instead
up to four repeats of the following: one access for one resource followed by five accesses for
the other resource. This pattern ends with a final access of the first resource.

5.3

Schedulability Results

We summarize the results across the full range of scenarios with the following observations.
▶ Observation 14. MultiResOpt is always best or tied for best.
As expected, no other approach outperforms MultiResOpt. This trend holds across all
results and is illustrated in Fig. 7.
▶ Observation 15. For some scenarios, the approach does significantly impact schedulability.
For some configurations, all approaches result in similar schedulability, even to NOLOCK.
One common pattern is the combination of medium per-task utilization and moderate task
periods, in which relatively few tasks are generated and the larger task periods imply larger
deadlines and WCETs. Because the access segment durations do not differ based on these
factors, the relative ratio of an individual access to the WCET is smaller.

Figure 8 Histogram of optimization solver runtimes for all task sets tested for Fig. 7a.

In some configurations, two or three approaches give similar results. One such example is
shown in Fig. 7b, in which MultiResOpt and GreedyNonNested result in very similar
schedulability. Here, each task has a single-resource probability of 0.85. In systems in which
all tasks use only a single resource, GreedyNonNested is optimal, so good schedulability
results could be expected with this high probability for single resource usage.
▶ Observation 16. The performance of GreedyNonNested varies based on the probability
of a task requesting only a single resource.
In general GreedyNonNested is a more effective approach in systems with higher
probability of a task using a single resource. Its performance relative to AlwaysCombine
depends on the configuration, as illustrated in Fig. 7. When the probability of a task using
only one resource is zero, GreedyNonNested is equivalent to NeverCombine under
alternating accesses and tends to be the worst approach.
▶ Observation 17. NeverCombine consistently yields among the worst schedulability.
This trend is illustrated in Fig. 7. Under the alternating access model, NeverCombine
has particularly lower schedulability relative to other approaches when the single-resource
probability is 0.85. For a task using a single resource, other approaches may combine many
accesses into a single critical section, reducing the overheads incurred and thus the WCET.

5.4

Runtime

Using MultiResOpt to determine critical sections for a given task set requires solving a
Quadratically-Constrained Integer Program for each resource-using task. To explore the
feasibility of this approach, we looked at the time taken to solve these problems. We used
the Gurobi optimization solver (version 9.1.2) [7] on a shared 2-socket machine with Intel
Xeon Gold 5218 CPUs at 2.30GHz, with access to 8 cores, 2 threads per core, and 16GB
memory. Fig. 8 presents the runtimes for all optimization problems that needed to be solved
for all task sets in Fig. 7a. Task sets that were unschedulable with NOLOCK were not
considered. As illustrated in Fig. 8, many problems can be solved in almost no time, and the
worst-case time scale is on the order of hundreds of milliseconds.

6

Extending to More Resources Per Task

In our formulation of the problem of how to group accesses into critical section as a
Quadratically-Constrained Integer Program, we limit each task to use at most two resources. We now explore the additional structure needed to support additional resources for a

ECRTS 2026


1:22

Critical-Section Granularity for Multi-Resource Systems

single task. We also present an alternate approach of enumerating all possible combinations,
which lends itself to simpler extension to more resources. Although such an enumeration is
computationally expensive, it is similar in spirit to recent work that enumerates a Schedule
Abstraction Graph [9] to determine schedulability.

6.1

Generalizing pre-designation of resource nesting order

The two-resource problem presented in Sec. 4.1 enabled choosing a single resource to be the
outer critical section when nesting occurs. We extend this to a multi-resource problem in which
a task uses two or more resources. This allows further development of an optimization-based
approach or pruning of an enumeration-based approach.
We say that two resources are adjacent if a critical section for one is nested within a
critical section for the other, and there is no intermediary critical section of a third resource
which contains the given critical section for one while nested within the given critical section
for the other. The definitions for valid grouping and optimal grouping can be generalized in
a straightforward way for a multi-resource setting. Note that the second observation in the
proof of Lem. 9 holds via similar reasoning even if a task utilizes an arbitrary number of
resources. We formalize this statement in the following corollary.
▶ Corollary 18. Suppose in a multi-resource problem that we have Qx ≥ Qy for resources ℒx
and ℒy . If the resources are adjacent, and a single critical section for resource ℒx is nested
within a critical section for ℒy , then an alternate solution with the critical section for ℒy
nested within a critical section for ℒx is valid and does not change C.
We say that resources ℒx and ℒy are inverted if Qx ≥ Qy and a critical section for ℒx is
nested inside one for ℒy . The following corollary is straightforward from the first observation
in the proof of Lem. 9.
▶ Corollary 19. Suppose a multi-resource problem admits an optimal grouping with nested
critical sections where for a particular critical section, ℒx and ℒy are inverted and adjacent.
Then all accesses for resource ℒx in that particular critical section must be grouped together.
▶ Corollary 20. If a multi-resource problem admits an optimal grouping with nested critical
sections, then there exists an optimal grouping such that no two resources are inverted.
Proof. For a given multi-resource problem, suppose we have an optimal grouping with a
nested critical section which has inverted resources. Using Cor. 18 and 19 we arrive at a
nested critical section without inverted resources by swapping inverted adjacent resources
without changing C. Applying this to every nested critical section with inverted resources
yields the desired result.
◀

6.2

Extending the optimization approach

The above results allow us to enforce a particular ordering on resource acquisition in nested
critical sections. This structure could form the basis for an extended optimization approach.
Note that its development would require adding variables and constraints to track nesting
and determine which resource(s) would be used in critical sections nested within others.
Alternatively, the above results give us the ability to prune an approach that would
otherwise consider all possible combinations of accesses into critical sections.


C. E. Nemitz, T. Amert, and J. Pulaj

Enumerating Possibilities

Here, we explore the full range of options for critical-section formation. Of these, we can
choose the one that minimizes task WCET while respecting the computed Qk values.
Consider a list ℒ ≜ [ℒ0 , ℒ1 , ℒ1 , . . . , ℒ0 ] with elements ℒ0 , ℒ1 in some order. Let [n] ≜
{1, 2, ..., n}, and let P([n]) denote the power set of [n] where elements in each set are ordered.
We outline a simple bijection between P([len(ℒ) − 1]) and the set of all possible critical
section arrangements (for now ignoring the additional potential arrangements in a properly
nested critical section). With every set S ∈ P([len(ℒ) − 1)]) we identify a list S consisting
of the elements of S in increasing order. The critical section arrangement identified with S
and therefore S is as follows. If S = ∅ then all elements of ℒ form a single critical section.
Otherwise, consider S[i] where i ∈ [len(S) − 1] ∪ {0}. The first critical section groups the first
ℒ[0], . . . , ℒ[S[0] − 1] elements together. In general for each i ∈ [len(S) − 1] a critical section
groups together elements ℒ[S[i − 1]], . . . , ℒ[S[i] − 1]. Finally the last critical section groups
together elements ℒ[S[len(S) − 1]], . . . , ℒ[len(ℒ) − 1]. This is a bijection by construction.

the critical section arrangement ℒ0 , ℒ1 ℒ1 , ℒ0 , ℒ1 . We identify the critical section arrangement with the following ordered collection of ordered sets (of positions) {{0}, {1, 2}, {3}, {4}}
denoted by 𝒜(ℒ){1,3,4} .
Given a critical section arrangement, we say that a critical section is monochromatic if
it contains only one resource. Given a list ℒ and a set S ∈ P([len(ℒ) − 1]), we say a set
B ∈ 𝒜(ℒ)S is monochromatic if its corresponding critical section is monochromatic. Define
𝒜(ℒ)S ≜ {B ∈ 𝒜(ℒ)S | |B| ≥ 3 and B is not monochromatic}. Given C ∈ 𝒜(ℒ)S , define

The enumeration approach can be extended to three resources. Consider for example ℒ =
[ℒ0 , ℒ1 , ℒ2 , ℒ0 , ℒ2 , ℒ1 , ℒ1 ]. Then consider one possible grouping of resources corresponding
to the collection 𝒜(ℒ){1,6} = {{0}, {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}, {6}}. In this case all extra cases to consider
come from {1, 2, 3, 4, 5} which corresponds to [ℒ1 , ℒ2 , ℒ0 , ℒ2 , ℒ1 ]. There are three choices for
the outer resource, namely ℒ0 , ℒ1 , ℒ2 , with the corresponding reduced blocks [ℒ1 , ℒ2 , ℒ2 , ℒ1 ],
[ℒ2 , ℒ0 , ℒ2 ], and [ℒ1 , ℒ0 , ℒ1 ]. Then, for each critical section with two resources we can
enumerate as previously.
The result from Sec. 6.1 allows us to prune the search space; based on the least constrained
bound on critical-section duration, we can choose which resource is for the outermost critical
section and ignore the other options without potentially eliminating all optimal solutions.

7

Conclusion

In this paper, we have generalized prior analysis for a single-resource system to a multiresource system. We then showed that the solution space for assigning accesses to critical
sections can be constrained based on bounds on the critical sections to designate one
resource to be the outer resource in any nested critical section. Using this, we developed a
Quadratically-Constrained Integer Program to model access-grouping decisions and resulting
critical-section durations and WCETs. We compared our approach to several heuristics on
the basis of schedulability, and we also looked at the runtime of solving these programs. We
then discussed an extension to support tasks with more resources.

ECRTS 2026


1:24

Critical-Section Granularity for Multi-Resource Systems

In the future, we plan to investigate further pruning that can be applied to the enumeration
approach. We also plan to generalize this approach to multiprocessors and investigate changing
task priorities. Additionally, we will explore the broader applicability of the fixed resource
nesting order. Our presented optimization approach relies on implications of using the PCP,
such as the ability to apply critical-section-duration bounds independently for each resource,
that may hold for other protocols as well. Finally, we plan to classify the scope of applicability
of our approach and extend it to support protocols with more complex requirements.

Abstract
We address the problem of scheduling periodic implicit-deadline real-time tasks on m uniform
processors. We introduce PCG∗ , an optimal TL-plane algorithm based on PCG [4], which guarantees
at most 2(m − 1) preemptions per TL-plane, matching the best-known theoretical bound for uniform
platforms. The proposed algorithm advances the state of the art by offering an optimal real-time
scheduling solution with a tight preemption bound within TL-planes. The numerical experiments
presented in this work provide strong evidence that PCG∗ yields a substantial reduction in the
number of preemptions relative to PCG. When applied to identical processor platforms, PCG∗ is
also a best-possible polynomial time algorithm in terms of preemptions in a TL-plane, matching the
(m − 1) preemption bound achieved by LRE-TL [9].

Keywords and phrases Real-Time Scheduling, Uniform Multiprocessor Platforms

1

Introduction

Modern real-time systems are increasingly deployed at the core of safety-critical and
performance-critical applications, from automotive and aerospace control to industrial automation and robotics. Guaranteeing that these systems always react within specified
deadlines, while at the same time making effective use of the available processing capacity,
requires the use of carefully designed scheduling algorithms supported by rigorous schedulability analysis. Such analysis techniques aim to characterize the worst-case timing behaviour
of real-time tasks under a given scheduling policy, and thereby provide a proof that all timing
constraints will be met during operation.
Multiprocessor platforms have become pervasive in real-time systems as modern workloads
(e.g., automotive, avionics, robotics, multimedia) exceed the capabilities of single-core
processors and power/thermal limits hinder further frequency scaling. Consequently, gaining
performance now relies on parallelism, which real-time scheduling and analysis must explicitly
account for to preserve timing guarantees. Moreover, heterogeneous architectures motivate

1

Corresponding author

© Yahya Hamdani, Pascal Richard, Antoine Bertout, Joël Goossens, and Emmanuel Grolleau;
licensed under Creative Commons License CC-BY 4.0
38th European Conference on Real-Time Systems (ECRTS 2026).
Editor: Angeliki Kritikakou; Article No. 2; pp. 2:1–2:23
Leibniz International Proceedings in Informatics
Schloss Dagstuhl – Leibniz-Zentrum für Informatik, Dagstuhl Publishing, Germany


2:2

Preempt Less, Schedule Better: Revisiting PCG for Real-Time Uniform Processors

the uniform-speed multiprocessor model, which captures different effective core capacities in
practical settings such as mixed-speed integration, reduced availability due to interference
or background services, incremental platform upgrades [2], DVFS/DVS operating modes
with speed–energy trade-offs [19, 24], and modern processors combining distinct core “types”,
reinforcing the need for schedulability methods that handle speed asymmetries [1, 21].
Among the large variety of real-time scheduling policies that have been proposed in the
literature, particular attention has been devoted to optimal algorithms, which are capable of
scheduling any task set that is feasible on a given platform. All currently known optimal
polynomial-time algorithms assume that task migrations and preemptions are performed
at no cost and incur no delay. The reason is that, once preemptions and migrations are
explicitly modelled as incurring non-zero delays, the problem complexity changes dramatically:
the resulting real-time scheduling problems become computationally hard, even on singlecore platforms. For example, the uniprocessor real-time scheduling problem with explicit
Cache-Related Preemption Delays (CRPD) has been shown to be strongly N P-hard, and
no online optimal algorithm exists [18]. This observation highlights why the zero-overhead
assumption is adopted when designing optimal multiprocessor schedulers. It is not merely
a technical convenience, but a fundamental requirement for obtaining optimal algorithms
with tractable schedulability tests. Understanding the capabilities and limitations of optimal
algorithms under this zero-overhead assumption is therefore a fundamental step both towards
clarifying the core combinatorial difficulties of real-time scheduling and towards bridging
the gap between theoretical optimality results and the behaviour of real systems, ultimately
enabling the design of scheduling algorithms and analysis techniques that incorporate realistic
operational constraints.
For multiprocessor systems, numerous optimal scheduling algorithms have been proposed [6]. Most of these algorithms target platforms with identical processors and task sets
composed of periodic tasks with implicit deadlines (i.e., each task must complete before its
next release). It is known that only global dynamic-priority scheduling algorithms (i.e., a job
priority may change during its execution) can achieve optimality in this setting, in the sense
that they can fully utilize all processors. In contrast, fixed-priority scheduling policies and
partitioned scheduling strategies have worst-case utilization bounds asymptotically limited
to 50%.
Notably, optimal algorithms based on DP-fair [15] principles (i.e., Deadline Partitioning
fair scheduling) like those based on the TL-plane abstraction [4, 5, 9, 10] (i.e., a TL-plane
defines a plane with Time and Local remaining execution times of jobs) decompose the
periodic task scheduling problem into independent time intervals, each bounded by successive
task releases/deadlines. Each interval then constitutes an independent subproblem, consisting
of a set of local jobs derived from the original periodic tasks. The objective within each
subproblem is to ensure that all local jobs complete before the next task deadline, which is
common to all local jobs.
In this paper, we focus on uniform multiprocessor systems, in which each processor may
operate at a different speed. Several optimal scheduling algorithms have been proposed in this
context, each capable of meeting all task deadlines for any feasible task set. More precisely,
we refine the PCG (Precaution Cut Greedy) online algorithm [4] so that it achieves the
best-known lower bound on the number of preemptions within a TL-plane. In this paper, we
introduce PCG∗ , an optimal TL-plane algorithm that guarantees at most 2(m−1) preemptions
per TL-plane, matching the best-known theoretical bound for uniform platforms [12]. To the
best of our knowledge, this is the first real-time scheduling algorithm that guarantees this
preemption bound. Furthermore, when restricted to identical processors, PCG∗ achieves the


Y. Hamdani, P. Richard, A. Bertout, J. Goossens, and E. Grolleau

2:3

best possible preemption bound of m − 1 [17], thereby matching the preemption bound of
the LRE-TL algorithm [9], which is designed for identical multiprocessors. The proposed
algorithm advances the state of the art by minimizing preemptions.

2

System model

We consider a set τ = {τ1 , . . . , τn } of independent sequential periodic real-time tasks to
be scheduled on a multiprocessor platform. Each task τj = (Cj , Tj ), for 1 ≤ j ≤ n, is
characterized by its worst-case execution time Cj ∈ R+ on a unit-speed processor and its
period Tj ∈ N, i.e., the interval between two consecutive job releases of τj . Each job of τj
must complete execution before the release of its next job, implying an implicit deadline.
C
The utilization factor of task τj is defined as uj = Tjj , representing the fraction of processing
capacity, on a unit-speed processor, required by τj over time. Tasks are synchronously
released at time 0.
An event-driven scheduler makes run-time decisions only when specific events occur: job
releases, completions, or deadlines. Each such scheduling event defines a scheduling point at
which the scheduler may select the jobs to execute.
A task set is said to be feasible if there exists a schedule in which every job completes
execution by its deadline. A scheduler is an algorithm that assigns tasks to processors for
execution. A scheduling algorithm is deemed optimal if it can successfully schedule every
feasible task set.
Our main objective was to define an optimal polynomial-time scheduling algorithm with
a guaranteed bound on the number of preemptions, which can only be achieved if preemption
overheads are not taken into account in the task model. Accordingly, we propose a scheduling
algorithm that does not consider such overheads.
In such scheduling algorithms, a job can be in one of three states: running if it is currently
executing on a processor, ready if it is eligible to execute but not assigned to any processor,
or completed. During execution, a job may be preempted on its current processor and later
resumed – possibly on a different processor, without incurring any overhead, since otherwise
no polynomial-time optimal scheduling algorithm can exist. Consequently, preemptions and
migrations are not distinguished and are collectively referred to as preemptions throughout this
paper, following the terminology used in job scheduling in operational research. This unified
terminology enables a direct comparison of scheduling algorithms from both communities
with respect to their preemption behaviour.
A processor πi , 1 ≤ i ≤ m, is characterized by its speed si ∈ R+ , representing the amount
of processing capacity provided per unit of time. If a task executes for d time units on
processor πi , it completes d × si units of execution. This model is referred to as a uniform
multiprocessor platform. When all processor speeds are identical, the platform is called an
identical multiprocessor platform, in which case we assume si = 1 for all i. We consider a
continuous-time model.

3

Bridging real-time and job scheduling

3.1

DP-Fair Schedules

Scheduling periodic tasks can be done by ensuring proportionate fair progression of tasks.
At any time, each task progresses at a constant rate corresponding to its utilization. This
means that, over any time interval of length ∆, task τi executes for exactly ui × ∆ time units,
where ui is its utilization factor. This theoretical abstraction of such an idealized execution
is referred to as a fluid schedule.

ECRTS 2026


2:4

Preempt Less, Schedule Better: Revisiting PCG for Real-Time Uniform Processors

While it is impossible to implement a truly fluid schedule at runtime, it is possible to approximate its behavior within fixed intervals, each bounded by consecutive releases/deadlines.
At each deadline, the schedule must have completed the same amount of work as the fluid
schedule. This approach is known as Deadline-Partitioning fair scheduling, or DP-fair for
short [15]. The same principle underlies TL-plane-based schedulers [4, 5], where each interval,
called a TL-plane, ensures that tasks make proportionate progress toward their deadlines.
This approach defines the class of DP-fair schedules.
The schedule to be defined within each interval is independent of the schedules in the
other intervals. In a given interval of length ∆, the portion l of the k th job, τi,k , corresponding
l
to task τi that must be executed is referred to as a local job τi,k
, with a local execution time,

denoted by pi,k , equal to pi,k = ui × ∆. It follows directly that, between the release time and
deadline of a job, which may span several successive intervals, the sum of the local execution
times of its corresponding local jobs is equal to the task’s worst-case execution time. Each
local job must be completed by time ∆, which is the common deadline for all local jobs
belonging to the same interval.
Let us consider a simple example adapted from [25] with two processors, π1 and π2 ,
with respective speeds s1 = 3 and s2 = 1, and two periodic tasks with implicit deadlines,
τ1 = (C1 = 40, T1 = 20) and τ2 = (C2 = 60, T2 = 30). The total utilization is U =
40/20 + 60/30 = 4, which is exactly equal to the platform capacity (i.e., s1 + s2 ). Because of
the processor speeds, this task set is not partitionable: neither task can be assigned entirely
to π2 , and no priority-driven policy can schedule them without allowing a task to execute
simultaneously on both processors over time. The only way to schedule these two tasks is to
share both processors equally within each time interval delimited by successive deadlines.

In Figure 1, the feasible DP-fair schedule pattern defined in [0, 20) is reused in every
subsequent interval, scaled according to the interval length. All local jobs belonging to the
same interval share a common deadline, namely the end of that interval. In the next interval,
[20, 30), the same schedule pattern is stretched to fit an interval of length 10. Note that local
job processing requirements are always proportional to the interval length. Therefore, the
pattern defined in the first interval can be reused with the corresponding local execution
times, and similarly in all subsequent intervals throughout the schedule. For this reason,
the feasibility analysis of a DP-fair schedule reduces to validating a single interval, in which
every local job shares a common deadline.
As a consequence, for a given interval of length ∆, the feasibility problem consists in
checking whether a set of local jobs can be scheduled within a time interval of length ∆, i.e.,
whether there exists a preemptive schedule whose makespan is less than or equal to ∆, where
the makespan is defined as the completion time of the last job in the schedule. Therefore,
the feasibility problem is equivalent to the well-known makespan minimization problem in
the operations research literature.

The principles of DP-fair schedules provide a straightforward decomposition method for
managing infinite schedules that arise from task periodicity. The schedule of local jobs within
each interval can be computed either online or offline. In the offline case, the schedule is
precomputed for a single interval and then stretched or replicated at runtime to fit subsequent
intervals. The offline schedule can also be computed at the beginning of each interval. In
both situations, however, an offline algorithm cannot account for variations in job execution
times at run-time. If an online algorithm is used instead, the computation can adapt to
variations in job execution times. Regardless of the scheduling approach used within each
interval, fairness is ensured at every deadline, since the local jobs have execution requirements
proportional to the length of the interval. Crucially, this approach reduces the infinite-horizon
feasibility problem to a finite makespan minimization problem within a single interval.

identical and uniform processors.

schedulable on an identical multiprocessor platform is given by [3]: ui ≤ 1, 1 ≤ i ≤ n and

Feasibility and makespan minimization equivalence. Due to the established equivalence
between the feasibility analysis of periodic task sets and the makespan minimization of local
jobs scheduled between two successive releases/deadlines in a DP-fair schedule, an optimal
real-time scheduling algorithm for periodic tasks with implicit deadlines must also optimally
solve the corresponding makespan minimization problem. Conversely, any algorithm that
optimally solves the makespan minimization problem can be used to construct a feasible
schedule for periodic tasks by replicating its execution pattern across successive intervals of
the infinite real-time schedule. This equivalence has been exploited to define DP-Wrap, a
simple yet effective algorithm for scheduling periodic tasks on identical processors, which
applies McNaughton’s wrap-around scheduling rule within each interval [15].

3.3

Scheduling algorithms

We next describe the two main approaches for optimally scheduling local jobs within an
interval bounded by two successive releases/deadlines.

3.3.1

Identical platforms

McNaughton’s algorithm [17] is a simple wrap-around rule. To construct a schedule of length
Cmax (as defined in Equation (1)), jobs are first sequenced in an arbitrary order on a single
virtual processor without any idle time. This single-processor schedule is then partitioned
into slices of duration Cmax , where the i-th slice defines the schedule of processor πi . Under
this construction, a job is preempted if and only if it spans across two consecutive slices,
meaning its execution is split between the end of the schedule on πi and the beginning of the
schedule on πi+1 , with no overlap.
The application of McNaughton’s rule to periodic task scheduling is known as DPWrap [15]. McNaughton’s algorithm guarantees that at most m − 1 preemptions can
occur [17], and this bound is tight. Moreover, it has been proven that constructing a
makespan-optimal schedule with fewer than (m − 1) preemptions is N P-hard [23].
Several online algorithms have also been proposed for identical processor platforms. The
Longest Remaining Processing Time (LRPT) rule is the simplest algorithm that is optimal
for minimizing the makespan [14]; it can be seen as the preemptive version of the Longest
Processing Time first scheduling rule. However, LRPT suffers from a major drawback: in
practice, it requires an infinite number of preemptions. Cascades of preemptions arise when
two or more jobs have exactly the same remaining execution time and must therefore be
executed at the same rate, as in the fluid schedule model. This issue can be circumvented by
applying the processor-sharing concept (for details, see [20]). Other algorithms have been


Y. Hamdani, P. Richard, A. Bertout, J. Goossens, and E. Grolleau

2:7

proposed in the real-time systems community, most notably TL-plane–based algorithms such
as LLREF [5] and LRE-TL [9]; their principles will be described in the next section. In
particular, LRE-TL guarantees no more than m − 1 migrations per TL-plane [9], thereby
matching the m − 1 preemption bound achieved by McNaughton’s algorithm.

3.3.2

Uniform platforms

Several offline algorithms have been proposed in the literature for minimizing the makespan.
Gonzalez and Sahni [12] introduced an O(n)-time algorithm for scheduling a set of jobs on
uniform processors, which minimizes the makespan while guaranteeing at most 2(m − 1)
preemptions. The algorithm assumes jobs and processors are sorted by non-increasing
execution time and speed, respectively. Jobs are then scheduled sequentially. Note that such
an offline algorithm cannot account for variations in job execution times at run-time.
This approach was later revisited in two significant works. In Martel’s paper [16], uniform
processors are modeled as a single composite processor with time-varying speed, consisting
of segments of constant speed within each interval of length Cmax defined in Equation (2). A
similar idea, based on multiple virtual processors with variable speeds, was proposed in [7].
Both algorithms are considerably easier to understand than the original method of Gonzalez
and Sahni.
The 2(m − 1) preemption bound is tight, as shown in [12]. Moreover, it has been
proven that constructing a schedule with fewer than 2(m − 1) preemptions is N P-hard [22].
Therefore, this bound constitutes the best possible guarantee achievable by any polynomialtime scheduling algorithm.
For online scheduling algorithms, the LRPT variant that assigns the job with the longest
remaining execution time to the fastest processors (LRPT-FM) is optimal for minimizing
the makespan, but it suffers from the same limitations as standard LRPT. The Level
algorithm [13] provides a better trade-off by ensuring at most n2 (m − 1) preemptions [12].
In the real-time systems community, two equivalent algorithms have been independently
proposed: PCG [4] and U-LLREF [10]. However, as we demonstrate in this paper, these
algorithms do not achieve the best possible preemption bound. In the following sections, we
present a detailed overview of TL-plane–based event-driven scheduling algorithms.

4

Principles of TL-plane algorithms

In the remainder of this paper, we focus on DP-fair schedules based on the TL-plane
abstraction [5]. As shown previously, both the feasibility analysis and the scheduling
algorithms are concerned with a single interval delimited by two successive releases/deadlines.
We formally proved in [11] that a deterministic DP-fair scheduler generates exactly the same
schedule pattern in every interval. Accordingly, the periodic task model is fully represented
by a set of local jobs, one for each original periodic task, together with their associated local
execution times. For the sake of simplicity, we hereafter refer to them simply as jobs and
execution times since we focus on a single TL-plane.
In the TL-plane abstraction, the progress of any job within an interval – bounded by two
successive releases/deadlines – can be represented in a two-dimensional plane, referred to as
the TL-plane. In this representation, the horizontal axis (T ) denotes time, while the vertical
axis (L) denotes the remaining execution time. As established earlier, the initial execution
time of the (local) job is equal to the TL-plane length multiplied by the job’s task utilization.
The first TL-plane–based algorithm, LLREF [5], is optimal for identical processor platforms. It follows the Longest Remaining Processing Time (LRPT) principle: at each
scheduling point, the m jobs with the longest remaining local execution times are assigned

ECRTS 2026


2:8

Preempt Less, Schedule Better: Revisiting PCG for Real-Time Uniform Processors

to the m processors until the next scheduling event occurs. These events define scheduling
points at which tasks are rescheduled according to LRPT. LRE-TL [9] improves upon LLREF
by applying LRPT only at the initialization of each TL-plane, rather than at every scheduling
point. Precisely, two types of scheduling events are defined. These types of events are
independent and may occur simultaneously2 :
Bottom event (B-event): occurs when a task completes, i.e., its local execution time
reaches 0.
Critical event (C-event): occurs when a task reaches zero laxity on a processor, i.e.,
the remaining execution time equals the remaining processor capacity available in the
TL-plane.
These ideas were extended to uniform processor platforms in [4]. Before presenting that
algorithm, called PCG, we first refine the definition of a C-event.
▶ Definition 1. A job i triggers a Ck -event at time t ≥ 0 if its remaining execution time at
t is exactly equal to the remaining processing capacity of processor πk over the interval [t, L),
where L denotes the schedule length. The remaining execution time at time t is defined by:
pi (t) = (L − t) sk ,
To avoid multiple preemptions, when a job triggers a Ck -event, PCG assigns the job to
processor πk for the remainder of the schedule. From that point on, it is never preempted.
From an implementation perspective, the job and its assigned processor are removed from
the corresponding lists of jobs and processors. The scheduling problem is thus decomposed
into a simpler subproblem for completing the schedule. PCG operates as follows [4]:
Initialization: Jobs are sorted in non-increasing order of their execution times, and
processors are sorted in non-increasing order of their speeds.
Main loop:
At any time t ≥ 0, upon each Ck -event, the corresponding job is permanently assigned
to πk for the remainder of the TL-plane. Both the job and the processor are then
removed from the scheduling problem.
At each B-event, the corresponding job is removed from the problem.
The remaining jobs are assigned to processors according to the LRPT-FM rule, until
the next event occurs.
